solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cool bat has admirers

explanation.surface: A cricket or baseball bat that is so stylish it has its own followers.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words read as adjective and noun, a cool bat, but each is a verb or thing in its own right: to fan cools, and a club is a bat.
explanation.definitionFit: The collective noun stands for the group: an organised body of devotees can be called simply its admirers.

clue.text: Ready to fart with much energy?

definitions.meaning: pulses are notorious for causing wind, so a stomach loaded with them is primed
an idiom for bouncy, lively high spirits

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about someone about to break wind.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude first reading is the literal one: a stomach full of beans. The idiom 'full of beans' means bursting with energy.
explanation.definitionFit: Literal and idiomatic senses: a belly stuffed with beans is primed for wind, and the everyday idiom means bouncy and lively.

clue.text: Family member's 'bon voyage' at last, with a sigh of relief

indicators.note: take the last letter of each word

parts.note: last letters of boN and voyagE
phew is what you say when relieved

explanation.surface: A relative's departure is waved off with a farewell and a relieved sigh.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a guest you were glad to see go; 'at last' looks like 'finally gone' but picks the last letters of both words.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: a brother's or sister's son is one particular relative.

clue.text: Secures mantles for portraits? No!

definitions.note: the definition works by contrast: landscape is the page orientation that is not portrait

parts.note: to land a deal is to secure it
a mantle is a cloak or cape

explanation.surface: Someone buying cloaks to dress sitters for their portraits, then thinking better of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Pictures and page layouts come in two orientations, portrait and landscape; the 'No!' turns portraits into their opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Defined by its opposite: pictures and page layouts are either tall portraits or wide scenes of countryside, so 'not portraits' points to the other kind.

clue.text: See 1
Water bird and water city

parts.note: a swan is a water bird

explanation.surface: A list of waterside things: a bird and a coastal city.
explanation.walkthrough: SWANSEA is a coastal city in south Wales. 'Water city' reads as one phrase, but 'water' belongs to the wordplay and 'city' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the Welsh port on the south coast is one example of a city.

clue.text: More palatable rugby formation? Mister, that is welcomed

parts.note: a scrum is a set formation in rugby

indicators.note: a host who welcomes a guest takes them inside

parts.note: Mr is the short form of Mister

explanation.surface: A rugby scrum is offered as tastier, and a man called Mister is made welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: SCRUMMY is informal British for delicious; the question mark flags the pun on scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British synonym: the comparative of scrummy, nursery slang for delicious, means tastier.

clue.text: Scotland's rising voice

indicators.note: the answer belongs to the word, sitting inside it
in a down clue the letters read upwards

explanation.surface: The voice of Scotland is rising, as in a national movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside SCOTLAND and read upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the low female or high male singing range is one of the voice parts in a choir.

clue.text: Careless error with footwear

parts.note: a slip is a small error

explanation.surface: A careless mistake made in the matter of shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Careless error' reads as one phrase, but 'Careless' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: originally wearing slippers, the word came to mean sloppy and slovenly.

clue.text: Story one acted out

indicators.note: out of order, so the letters are put out of their places

explanation.surface: A story that one person performed in front of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acted out' looks like one phrasal verb, but 'out' alone is the instruction and 'acted' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a short personal tale told in conversation is a story.

clue.text: Type of flower or 4
Refreshes vehicle for military attack

parts.note: to air a room is to freshen it

explanation.surface: A vehicle is spruced up for an offensive.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces do not match the answer's two words: the S of the first word is borrowed by the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a bombing raid from aircraft is one kind of military attack.

clue.text: Starts Google at last with identical password

indicators.note: 'at last' means at the very end, so only Google's end letter is used

explanation.surface: Someone starting up Google and using the same password again.
explanation.walkthrough: Open sesame is the magic password from Ali Baba; the web-login surface hides that.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the magic words that open the robbers' cave in Ali Baba are the most famous password in fiction.

clue.text: Occasionally unsteady? That's not new

indicators.note: every other letter, only now and then

explanation.surface: Something wobbly now and then, which is no surprise since it is not new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' looks like an adverb about wobbling; it picks every other letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: second-hand goods have had an owner before, so are not new.

clue.text: Antagonism for one appearing in this theatrical production

parts.note: the nativity play put on by schools at Christmas

explanation.surface: Someone's hostility on show in a stage production.
explanation.walkthrough: A nativity play is the Christmas story staged, usually by schoolchildren.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a hostile, opposing attitude is antagonism.

clue.text: Epic march in which one's gone astray

explanation.surface: A long march during which someone wanders off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Epic march' reads as a long trek, but 'Epic' is the definition: Milton's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: Milton's twelve-book poem of the Fall is the great English epic.

clue.text: Not well kept by vessel with guns

explanation.surface: A sick sailor held aboard a warship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel with guns' reads as a warship; the vessel is a blood vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Collective synonym: large-calibre mounted weapons, taken together, are an army's big guns.

clue.text: Contender's sea trawler dismissed as out of order

indicators.note: sent away, like a player dismissed from the field, so the A's leave the fodder

parts.note: remove the As, the two letter A's

explanation.surface: A fishing boat owned by a competitor is condemned as broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' reads as a plain conjunction, but here it is A's, the two letter As to drop from SEA TRAWLER.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a grappler in the ring is one kind of contender.

clue.text: Making sense of some arithmetic

definitions.meaning: said of an explanation that hangs together
totting a column of figures together

explanation.surface: Someone trying to understand a sum.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, understanding maths; it splits into two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: figuratively a story that hangs together, literally summing numbers.

clue.text: Ground ready to welcome landlord, finally invited for special occasion

indicators.note: ground as in ground down, so READY is crushed into new order

parts.note: a landlord lets property, so is one who lets

indicators.note: 'finally' means at the end, so only the end letter of the next word counts

explanation.surface: A prepared field awaits the landlord, the last to be invited to a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a noun, a sports ground, but it is the past participle of grind. The landlord trick is worth learning: one who lets is a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: saints' days were printed in red in church calendars, so a memorable day is marked out as special.

clue.text: Part of the Bible left wrapped up in thirty seconds? Not by him!

definitions.note: an extended cross-reference: Milton wrote Paradise Lost (14 across) but not the Bible

parts.note: half a minute is half of MINUTE, MIN

explanation.surface: A pious aside: a bit of scripture is packed in half a minute, and the writer disowns it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thirty seconds' is half of a minute, so half the word MINUTE. The exclamation says Milton wrote a biblical epic but not the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: John Milton was a poet, famously not the Bible's author though he retold Genesis.

clue.text: Story of Romeo: literary cliché coming up

parts.note: Romeo is R in the phonetic alphabet
a trope is a stock literary device

explanation.surface: Romeo's tale is full of worn-out literary devices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Story of Romeo' makes you think of Shakespeare; 'Story' alone is the definition and Romeo is just R.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalistic synonym: a news item filed by a reporter is a story.

clue.text: High and mighty people rejected shady character

indicators.note: sent back, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: Important people turn away a dodgy type.
explanation.walkthrough: A spiv is British slang for a flashy petty crook, the wartime black-market dealer.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang: the flashily dressed wartime black-market dealer is a byword for a shady character.

clue.text: Putty shaped in its place

indicators.note: the letters are moulded into a new form

explanation.surface: Putty pressed into its proper spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The indicator suits the answer: plasticine is exactly what you shape. Putty is used loosely for any soft modelling paste.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: the children's modelling clay is soft and pliable like putty.

clue.text: Kind of bush? That's about right

parts.note: the word itself, referred to by 'That'

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a plant is a type of bush and is told that's roughly correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' points back to the word BUSH, which is reused on purpose as fodder; 'about right' sounds like approximate agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Near synonym: a low woody plant with many stems is what gardeners call a bush.

clue.text: Male 50 per cent of students

indicators.note: fifty per cent is a half, so only half the word's letters are kept

explanation.surface: A statistic: half of all students are men.
explanation.walkthrough: STUDENTS has eight letters, and the first four make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is a male animal kept for breeding, or a virile man.

clue.text: A long way from Blighty earthenware

indicators.note: the letters are taken from the words that follow

explanation.surface: Pottery shipped from home, a long way off.
explanation.walkthrough: Blighty is old British slang for Britain, home to soldiers abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Unit as distance: the distance light travels in a year, nearly six trillion miles, is a very long way.

clue.text: Back in a fortnight for the overture

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the word

explanation.surface: Returning in two weeks' time in order to hear the opening music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in a fortnight' reads as a promise to return; it hides the answer backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: the clipped form of introduction means the opening piece of music.

clue.text: Fast kind of music, with nonchalance

parts.note: idly = in a casual, unconcerned way

explanation.surface: A style of music played quickly but in a laid-back way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast kind of music' reads as one phrase, but 'Fast' stands alone as an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, both adverbs: to run fast is to run at speed.

clue.text: A boy, ten playing with weapon

indicators.note: the letters play around into a new order

explanation.surface: A ten-year-old boy playing with a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The worrying image is the disguise: 'playing' is the instruction to rearrange A BOY TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the blade fixed to a rifle's muzzle is a weapon.
